title: The economics of Jensen Huang
content:
Most of my assessment is very positive, but I will excerpt this bit from my latest Free Press piece:

Finally, the company was not built to withstand Huang’s departure. Too much authority and knowledge were concentrated in his hands, as evidenced by his practice of having about 60 different people reporting directly to him. Whatever you may think of that system as a day-to-day routine, it can turn disastrous when the person at the top leaves. No one else has collected and interpreted the information those 60 subordinates have imparted to the CEO. We will see how his interim successor Colette Kress does, but there is a great danger that a lot of the contextual understanding of the company and business departed with Huang.

Again, all those direct reports may have worked wonderfully when things were going great, but as a more general practice it is not resilient. Another way to put the point is that the very best CEOs make themselves at least partially dispensable, rather than indispensable. So a large share price decline, following Huang’s resignation, is a sign of his failures as well as his successes. As one set of commentators wrote recently: “the company was never built for him not to be there.”

And one of the very best Ben Thompson columns (gated!) is on Huang and Nvidia.
